newsitem.title: CHINA: China looks to future by backing Thailand bailout.
newsitem.headline: China looks to future by backing Thailand bailout.

text.p: Beijing's pledge to pump $1.0 billion into a regional financial bailout for Thailand shows China is determined to boost international cooperation as its economy opens to the outside world, analysts said on Thursday.

Central bank governor Dai Xianglong said he notified the International Monetary Fund late on Wednesday that China would be part of a $16 million IMF-led loan package aimed at helping Thailand out of its current economic crisis.

"This package planned for Thailand by the IMF and Asian countries is good for stability in the Asian and international economies... This method is absolutely essential," Dai told reporters after a news conference in Beijing.
Market pressure forced financially battered Thailand to float the baht last month in what amounted to a devaluation for the one-time tiger economy.
The crisis helped to increase pressure on other Southeast Asian currencies and prompted the IMF to mastermind the bailout package to try to restore international confidence.

While China has retained tight control of capital transfers, rendering it largely immune to the instability in Southeast Asian currencies, analysts said Dai's $1.0 billion pledge showed Beijing was already looking to the future.

China had freed foreign exchange under the current account and would face increased pressures on its currency as it moved toward freedom under the capital account, so helping Thailand now was a wise decision, said Jason Kwok, chief China economist at Citibank in Hong Kong.
"It's a good move as far as contributing to maintaining stability in the regional currency market in preparation for their own opening up in the future," Kwok said.

Beijing was determined to increase its involvement in international financial cooperation and the size of its pledge to Thailand would help to build up diplomatic capital for the future, said one diplomat in the Chinese capital.
"One can look at it as evidence of commitment or solidarity," the diplomat said. "It's an interesting development... a really encouraging one."
People's Bank of China governor Dai said his main aim was to preserve international currency stability, but made clear diplomacy was also a factor in the loan pledge.
"China and Thailand are friendly neighbouring countries," he said but did not elaborate.

The scale of China's assistance was well behind the $4.0 billion promises made by the IMF and Japan, but put Beijing in the second tier of assistance along with economies such as Australia, Singapore and Hong Kong that are seen as richer.
The size of China's pledge reflected its powerful recent growth, hefty foreign exchange reserves and the sheer size of its economy, said one Western economist.
"Some people wonder why one of the poorest countries in the region is contributing, but on the other hand I think this does show China's role as an economic power," the economist said.
Joining the bailout would be unlikely to turn out to be an expensive decision for Beijing, which could expect its loan to generate interest at close to market rates, he said.
"This is really not money they are putting at great risk," he said. "At the worst case they are going to lose out on interest... It is not like giving food out of the people's mouths."
